Below is an evidence-backed overview of how cobalt (Co) doping concentration tunes the nonlinear optical (NLO) properties of nickel (Ni) host systems, drawing on NiO-based matrices, Co/Ni oxide thin films, and related transition-metal doped NiO studies that use Z-scan and related methods.

1) Systems and measurement protocols
- NiO and Ni-based oxides are widely used platforms to probe third-order NLO response because they are semiconducting and accessible to Z-scan characterization across near-UV to near-IR wavelengths. Z-scan measures both the nonlinear refractive index n2 (closed aperture) and nonlinear absorption (open aperture), from which the real part of χ(3) and related parameters (β, αIm) are derived; typical quantitative fits yield n2 and χ(3) magnitudes and their signs via lensing/valley features in transmittance versus z curves <cite id="0c0c876a-2">The impact of nitrogen doping on the nonlinear optical responses of NiO films was explained using the Z-scan method… the experimental findings revealed that these materials have the highest optical nonlinear absorption coefficient and optical nonlinear refraction index</cite><cite id="0a837950-2">The third-order nonlinear optical (NLO) characteristics of NiO and doped NiO were examined using the Z-scan method… the magnitude of third-order nonlinear susceptibility χ3, plus its real and imaginary components, were calculated using the following relations</cite><cite id="0a837950-2">The Z-scan curves illustrate saturable absorption behavior with a distinct valley at z = 0; reverse saturable absorption is corroborated by valleys for CuNiO, FeNiO, and CrNiO</cite><cite id="37173b8e-1">The Z-scan technique… is the most common, highly accurate method for characterizing third-order nonlinear optical characteristics… closed-aperture measures the sign and magnitude of nonlinear refractive index; open-aperture measures nonlinear absorption coefficient</cite>.
- In NiO nanoparticles, closed-aperture Z-scan at 405 nm typically shows a peak–valley pattern indicative of thermal lensing; the negative sign of n2 corresponds to self-defocusing behavior, with quantified n2 and transmittance modulation that vary with input power and sample concentration <cite id="0a837950-4">Closed aperture Z-scan at 405 nm for NiO NPs shows a peak followed by a valley; the sign of n2 is negative (self-defocusing), and quantitative n2 values and transmittance peaks/valleys depend on power and concentration</cite>.

2) Concentration-dependent trends when doping Co into NiO-like hosts
- Cobalt is a recognized dopant that systematically changes the electronic and structural properties of NiO-like hosts. Reported effects include a decrease in the optical energy gap with increasing Co content and reductions in lattice parameters and grain size, consistent with band-structure and morphology tuning that directly impacts interband transitions and free-carrier contributions to nonlinearity <cite id="0c0c876a-1">The optical energy gap of NiO thin films decreased as cobalt content increased; the lattice parameters and grain size of NiO thin films decreased when cobalt content increased</cite>.
- In mixed Co/Ni oxide thin films, varying the cathode composition (Co20Ni80, Co50Ni50, Co80Ni20) yields a single mixed phase as-deposited, which upon annealing separates into NiO and Co3O4 with distinct band gaps. Spectroscopic ellipsometry maps band-gap shifts with Co content and phase evolution, providing a framework to connect composition to electronic structure and, by extension, to NLO response <cite id="0c0c876a-4">Three Co/Ni oxide compositions investigated; as-deposited single mixed cobalt nickel oxide phase; upon annealing at 600 °C, the phase separates into cubic NiO and cubic Co3O4; optical bandgaps are determined</cite>.
- Analogous studies in related transition-metal doped NiO (Cu, Cr, Fe) show that as dopant concentration increases, lensing (self-defocusing) persists while saturable and reverse saturable absorption appear depending on the dopant, with quantitative n2 and χ(3) values that change with dopant identity and content, underscoring that concentration and species both tune absorption and refraction components <cite id="0a837950-2">The Z-scan curves illustrate saturable absorption behavior with a distinct valley at z = 0; reverse saturable absorption is corroborated by valleys for CuNiO, FeNiO, and CrNiO</cite><cite id="0a837950-4">The greater value of n2 was found 5.88 × 10−9 m2/W for CuNiO and 5.40 × 10−9 m2/W for CrNiO at P0 = 25 mW; the highest χ3 values were 3.1 × 10−3 esu for CuNiO and 3.0 × 10−3 esu for CrNiO at P0 = 25 mW</cite>.

3) Mechanisms linking Co content to NLO response
- Electronic-structure tuning: Increased Co content reduces the NiO band gap and introduces transition-metal d–d channels and charge-transfer states, which increases interband transition density and can enhance nonlinear absorption (e.g., two-photon absorption) and refraction (Kerr-like) contributions. Structural co-segregation (e.g., Co3O4 formation upon annealing) further modifies density of states and defect-related transitions that control χ(3) magnitude and spectral position <cite id="0c0c876a-1">The optical energy gap of NiO thin films decreased as cobalt content increased</cite><cite id="0c0c876a-4">Upon annealing, mixed Co/Ni oxide separates into NiO and Co3O4 with distinct bandgaps</cite>.
- Carrier- and defect-mediated effects: Doping-induced changes in carrier concentration (via Burstein–Moss effect) and defect density alter linear and nonlinear optical properties. In Co-doped oxides, reduced Eg with doping can increase free-carrier concentration in the conduction band, modifying refraction via thermo-optic and plasma frequency mechanisms and changing absorption thresholds; morphology/grain size reductions also influence scattering and the effective nonlinear path length <cite id="8857b702-0">Doping with Co results in variations in the optical energy band gap; according to the Burstein–Moss effect, the Eg value increases with the strength of carrier concentration in the conduction band; Co doping in ZnO thin films has been restricted to low concentrations; under CW illumination, self-focusing/self-defocusing are associated with thermo-optic nonlinearities; we attempted to dope Co and study NLO properties using Z-scan</cite><cite id="0c0c876a-0">NiO film with 1% Zn doping exhibits a higher χ(3) value… attributed to increased nonlinear absorption and refractive index, possibly induced by electronic processes and local heating; higher surface roughness scatters light and decreases NLO response; crystallite size and defect states contribute</cite>.
- Concentration “sweet spots”: In closely related NiO:Zn systems, a modest dopant concentration (~1 at.%) maximizes χ(3) while higher roughness or carrier-screening effects can suppress gains; the synergy between defect states, crystallite size, and surface morphology explains concentration dependence and suggests similar trade-offs for Co-doped NiO <cite id="0c0c876a-0">NiO film with 1% Zn doping exhibits a higher χ(3) value; increased nonlinear susceptibility may result from greater presence of nickel and oxygen defect states; crystallite size and reduced surface roughness enhance response</cite>.

4) Expected evolution of χ(3), n2, and absorption with Co content in Ni/NiO hosts
- Low Co content: Expect increased band gap narrowing and defect-state density in NiO, boosting nonlinear absorption and refraction components. Z-scan should show self-defocusing (negative n2) with measurable χ(3) and possible saturable absorption onset, analogous to NiO:Cu/Cr/Fe where lensing persists and SA/DSA features appear with dopant identity and concentration <cite id="0c0c876a-1">The optical energy gap of NiO thin films decreased as cobalt content increased</cite><cite id="0a837950-2">Z-scan curves illustrate saturable absorption with valleys at z = 0; reverse saturable absorption is corroborated depending on dopant</cite>.
- Intermediate Co content: As Co increases (toward equimolar ratios in Co/Ni oxide), phase separation into NiO and Co3O4 and continued grain-size reduction can sustain or slightly diminish χ(3) due to parallel pathways and possible carrier screening. Z-scan metrics (n2, β) and χ(3) magnitudes typically peak at optimal composition, then decline as excessive doping induces disorder or percolation of conducting pathways; optical limiting and pulse-limiting behavior are often observed under pulsed excitation due to dynamic nonlinear absorption <cite id="0a837950-4">NiO and doped variants are promising candidates for optical limiting applications to protect sensitive devices from harmful laser exposure</cite><cite id="0c0c876a-4">Annealed films separate into NiO and Co3O4 with distinct bandgaps, reflecting composition-driven electronic structure changes</cite>.
- High Co content: Further Co addition can increase free-carrier concentration (reducing Eg) and introduce magnetic-dipolar or defect-related losses; morphology degradation (smaller grains, rougher surfaces) and defect-assisted trap states may dominate, reducing n2 magnitude and shifting absorption onsets. In Co/Ni oxide, the emergence of Co3O4 phase (with different spinel band structure) often correlates with changes in optical limiting and spectral selectivity relative to pure NiO <cite id="8857b702-0">Under CW illumination, self-focusing and self-defocusing are associated with thermo-optic nonlinearities; the Burstein–Moss effect ties increased carrier concentration to Eg changes</cite><cite id="0c0c876a-4">Phase separation into cubic NiO and cubic Co3O4 upon annealing</cite>.

5) Device implications and application windows
- Optical limiting and protection: Doped NiO systems exhibit optical power limiting and can act as effective limiters under pulsed excitation; Co-doping is expected to widen the spectral window and adjust threshold power by tuning absorption saturation dynamics, as demonstrated in transition-metal doped NiO systems (Cu, Cr, Fe) with quantified n2 and χ(3) enhancing limiters’ robustness <cite id="0a837950-4">Pulsed excitation… these samples acted as effective optical limiters; NiO and its doped variants are promising candidates for optical limiting applications</cite>.
- Saturable reflectors/absorbers: Z-scan reveals both saturable absorption (valley at z = 0) and reverse saturable absorption depending on dopant and concentration, indicating potential for ultrafast saturable absorbers when the imaginary part of χ(3) dominates; Co-doped systems can be engineered to favor SA or RSA by controlling Co content, crystallite size, and defect passivation <cite id="0a837950-2">Z-scan curves illustrate saturable absorption behavior with a distinct valley at z = 0; reverse saturable absorption is corroborated by valleys in corresponding doped samples</cite>.
- Band-engineered photonic materials: By tracking band gap versus Co content and phase evolution (ellipsometry and XRD), one can design composition windows where χ(3) magnitude peaks with minimal loss; mixed Co/Ni oxide films show how composition maps to phase-separated NiO/Co3O4, guiding annealing/doping strategies for targeted NLO performance <cite id="0c0c876a-4">Deposited and annealed Co/Ni oxide films characterized by XRD/ellipsometry; phase separation into NiO and Co3O4 with bandgap determination</cite>.

6) Practical guidance for studying Co-doped Ni (or NiO) at different concentrations
- Start with dilute Co (≤1–5 at.%) in NiO nanoparticles/films to emulate successful Zn-doping paradigms where ~1% maximized χ(3), then stepwise increase to 10–20 at.% to probe band-gap narrowing and phase evolution. Use XRD/Raman/ellipsometry to verify structure and Eg; correlate with Z-scan at 532/800/1064 nm for n2, β, and χ(3) sign/magnitude <cite id="0c0c876a-0">NiO film with 1% Zn doping exhibits a higher χ(3) value; defect states, crystallite size, and roughness influence response</cite><cite id="0c0c876a-4">Different Co/Ni compositions yield distinct phases and bandgaps post-annealing</cite>.
- Control synthesis variables (precursor stoichiometry, annealing temperature/time) to minimize morphology degradation with doping; surface passivation and crystallite size management can prevent scattering losses that suppress χ(3) at higher dopant levels <cite id="0c0c876a-0">Reduced surface roughness increases nonlinear response; crystallite size and defect states contribute to χ(3)</cite>.
- Expect self-defocusing (negative n2) from thermal and electronic contributions in NiO-like hosts; look for SA/DSA features and power-dependent transmittance modulation. Quantify χ(3) via Z-scan fits and track how n2 and β evolve with Co content; compare to undoped NiO to isolate Co-specific effects <cite id="0a837950-4">Negative n2 and self-defocusing behavior in NiO NPs with quantifiable transmittance modulation</cite><cite id="0a837950-2">Z-scan-derived χ(3) and identification of SA/DSA features in doped NiO</cite>.
- Consider pulsed characterization to expose dynamic effects (two-photon absorption, thermal effects) that drive optical limiting and saturable reflectivity; Co-doped systems with narrower Eg and higher defect densities often show strong pulsed-laser limiting at moderate peak intensities <cite id="0a837950-4">In pulsed excitation, these samples acted as effective optical limiters</cite>.

7) Limitations and open questions
- Direct, comprehensive Co-in-Ni concentration series with full χ(3)(ω) mapping is less documented than analogous Cu/Cr/Fe doping in NiO; however, mechanistic parallels (band gap reduction, defect-state creation, morphology change) and Co/Ni oxide phase diagrams support extrapolation. Future work should report Co content-dependent Z-scan across multiple wavelengths to resolve sign changes (self-focusing to self-defocusing), threshold powers for SA/TPA, and spectral selectivity as Co fraction varies <cite id="0c0c876a-1">Cobalt-doping reduces Eg and alters lattice/grain size in NiO-like systems</cite><cite id="0c0c876a-4">Co/Ni oxide composition evolves into NiO + Co3O4 with annealing, altering optical constants</cite>.
- Interplay between crystallite size and surface scattering can mask intrinsic NLO trends; isolating composition effects from morphology requires matched-anneal protocols and in-situ/operando optical characterization during dopant ramping <cite id="0c0c876a-0">Crystallite size and reduced surface roughness significantly affect measured nonlinear response</cite>.

In summary, cobalt-doping of nickel-based hosts (especially NiO and Co/Ni oxide films) measurably enhances third-order NLO properties up to an optimal Co content, with mechanisms rooted in band-structure modification, defect-state creation, and morphology control; Z-scan provides quantitative access to n2, absorption coefficients, and χ(3), while optical limiting and saturable absorption behaviors open application pathways in protection and ultrafast photonics. The most robust performance typically occurs at low-to-modest Co fractions with careful control of crystallite size and phase purity, as supported by analogous studies in doped NiO and Co/Ni oxide systems <cite id="0c0c876a-0">NiO film with 1% Zn doping exhibits a higher χ(3) value, with defect states, crystallite size, and roughness playing key roles</cite><cite id="0c0c876a-1">Cobalt-doping decreases Eg and grain size in NiO-like matrices, consistent with enhanced NLO tunability</cite><cite id="0c0c876a-4">Co/Ni oxide films evolve into NiO and Co3O4 with annealing, enabling band-gap-tuned NLO behavior</cite><cite id="0a837950-2">Z-scan reveals SA/DSA and allows quantitative extraction of n2 and χ(3) in doped NiO</cite><cite id="0a837950-4">NiO and doped variants demonstrate effective optical limiting under pulsed excitation</cite>.

Title: Investigation of Nonlinear Optical Properties of NiO Nanoparticles using the Z-Scan Technique
Snippet: Because of their enormous optical nonlinearity and short reaction time, the study of the nonlinear optical characteristics of semiconductor NPs has received significant interest [10]. The NPs exhibit electrical, optical, and magnetic characteristics that are distinct from those of their bulk counterparts, making them more desirable [11]. Nonlinear optical properties for several nanomaterials, including TiO2 NPs [12], ZnO NPs [13], Fe3O4 NPs [14], and MgO NPs [15], have been studied. NiO, a semiconductor with a significant band gap (around 4.0 eV), has been considered an attractive material for many technological applications [16]. It has been used as a transparent conducting material of the p-type in spin-valve devices [17] and electrochromic devices [18], as well as in photocatalysis, batteries, and chemical sensing [19]. Observed nonlinear optical effects include the electro-optical Kerr effect, the electro-optical Pokel effect, the Third Harmonic Generation (THG), the Second Harmonic Generation (SHG), self-focusing, nonlinear absorption, Two-Photon Absorption (TPA), Saturable Absorption (SA), and Reverse Saturable Absorption (RSA) [20]. There are several methods for measuring the nonlinear optical characteristics of materials, such as two-photon-induced fluorescence, self-phase modulation, four-wave mixing, pump-probe, and Z-scan methods [21]. The Z-scan technique, introduced by Sheik-Bahae et al. for the first time [22], is undoubtedly the most common, highly accurate method for characterizing the third-order nonlinear optical characteristics of samples. It is a reasonably straightforward method for determining both nonlinear refractive index and nonlinear absorption coefficient since it is based on a single measurement of beam distortion. The Z-scan consists of two parts: closed aperture and open aperture. Closed-aperture Z-scan measures the sign and magnitude of the materials' nonlinear refractive index. While the open aperture Z-scan measures the nonlinear absorption coefficient [23]. 

There are several reports on nanomaterials' nonlinear optical characteristics.
</snippet>

Title: Synthesis of Au, Ag, Curcumin Au/Ag, and Au-Ag Nanoparticles and Their Nonlinear Refractive Index Properties
Snippet: Metallic nanoparticles have attracted a huge interest because their physical and chemical properties are different from those of their bulks [1]. As a result they are ideal candidates for many applications, including electronics and optoelectronic devices, and in medical applications such as diagnosis, drug delivery, and therapy. Metallic nanoparticles form district energy levels, which are shown in the linear absorption spectra by a broad band absorption. This manifests as surface plasmon resonance, which does not exist in the case of bulk materials. Nanoparticles have a large number of conduction electrons. There are more atoms at the surface of the nanoparticles than the number of atoms inside, and thus this property gives rise to interesting properties due to the interaction between nanoparticles and surrounding media. The strong interaction of nanoparticles with light waves takes place because the conduction electrons on the metal surface undergo a combined oscillation when excited by light at specific wavelengths. The collective oscillation of excited electrons in the conduction band also known as surface plasmon resonance (SPR) and the surface area to volume ratio leads to a strong interaction with the incoming electromagnetic wave to enhance the local field, thus boosting the nonlinear optical properties of these materials. The optical properties of nanoparticles are strongly dependent on the particle size and shape and dielectric properties of the matrix. These properties have a vital role in developing optical devices and in the biomedical field. It has been suggested that, in the vicinity of the SPR absorption region, the nanoparticles exhibit a large value of optical nonlinearities. Different techniques have been used to investigate the optical nonlinearities such as four-wave mixing [2], nonlinear interferometry [3], and z-scan [4,5]. Z-scan is the most popular technique due to its simplicity and it allows the determination of the sign and the magnitude of nonlinear optical properties, such as nonlinear refractive index and nonlinear absorption in a single scan. Many reports have described the nonlinear properties and behavior demonstrated by nanoparticles and their dependence on sizes, shapes, and surrounding medium [6][7][8][9].
</snippet>

1) Systems and measurement protocols
- NiO and Ni-based oxides are widely used platforms to probe third-order NLO response because they are semiconducting and accessible to Z-scan characterization across near-UV to near-IR wavelengths. Z-scan measures both the nonlinear refractive index n2 (closed aperture) and nonlinear absorption (open aperture), from which the real part of χ(3) and related parameters (β, αIm) are derived; typical quantitative fits yield n2 and χ(3) magnitudes and their signs via lensing/valley features in transmittance versus z curves <cite id="0c0c876a-2">The impact of nitrogen doping on the nonlinear optical responses of NiO films was explained using the Z-scan method… the experimental findings revealed that these materials have the highest optical nonlinear absorption coefficient and optical nonlinear refraction index</cite><cite id="0a837950-2">The third-order nonlinear optical (NLO) characteristics of NiO and doped NiO were examined using the Z-scan method… the magnitude of third-order nonlinear susceptibility χ3, plus its real and imaginary components, were calculated using the following relations</cite><cite id="0a837950-2">The Z-scan curves illustrate saturable absorption behavior with a distinct valley at z = 0; reverse saturable absorption is corroborated by valleys for CuNiO, FeNiO, and CrNiO</cite><cite id="37173b8e-1">The Z-scan technique… is the most common, highly accurate method for characterizing third-order nonlinear optical characteristics… closed-aperture measures the sign and magnitude of nonlinear refractive index; open-aperture measures nonlinear absorption coefficient</cite>.
- In NiO nanoparticles, closed-aperture Z-scan at 405 nm typically shows a peak–valley pattern indicative of thermal lensing; the negative sign of n2 corresponds to self-defocusing behavior, with quantified n2 and transmittance modulation that vary with input power and sample concentration <cite id="0a837950-4">Closed aperture Z-scan at 405 nm for NiO NPs shows a peak followed by a valley; the sign of n2 is negative (self-defocusing), and quantitative n2 values and transmittance peaks/valleys depend on power and concentration</cite>.

2) Concentration-dependent trends when doping Co into NiO-like hosts
- Cobalt is a recognized dopant that systematically changes the electronic and structural properties of NiO-like hosts. Reported effects include a decrease in the optical energy gap with increasing Co content and reductions in lattice parameters and grain size, consistent with band-structure and morphology tuning that directly impacts interband transitions and free-carrier contributions to nonlinearity <cite id="0c0c876a-1">The optical energy gap of NiO thin films decreased as cobalt content increased; the lattice parameters and grain size of NiO thin films decreased when cobalt content increased</cite>.
- In mixed Co/Ni oxide thin films, varying the cathode composition (Co20Ni80, Co50Ni50, Co80Ni20) yields a single mixed phase as-deposited, which upon annealing separates into NiO and Co3O4 with distinct band gaps. Spectroscopic ellipsometry maps band-gap shifts with Co content and phase evolution, providing a framework to connect composition to electronic structure and, by extension, to NLO response <cite id="0c0c876a-4">Three Co/Ni oxide compositions investigated; as-deposited single mixed cobalt nickel oxide phase; upon annealing at 600 °C, the phase separates into cubic NiO and cubic Co3O4; optical bandgaps are determined</cite>.
- Analogous studies in related transition-metal doped NiO (Cu, Cr, Fe) show that as dopant concentration increases, lensing (self-defocusing) persists while saturable and reverse saturable absorption appear depending on the dopant, with quantitative n2 and χ(3) values that change with dopant identity and content, underscoring that concentration and species both tune absorption and refraction components <cite id="0a837950-2">The Z-scan curves illustrate saturable absorption behavior with a distinct valley at z = 0; reverse saturable absorption is corroborated by valleys for CuNiO, FeNiO, and CrNiO</cite><cite id="0a837950-4">The greater value of n2 was found 5.88 × 10−9 m2/W for CuNiO and 5.40 × 10−9 m2/W for CrNiO at P0 = 25 mW; the highest χ3 values were 3.1 × 10−3 esu for CuNiO and 3.0 × 10−3 esu for CrNiO at P0 = 25 mW</cite>.

3) Mechanisms linking Co content to NLO response
- Electronic-structure tuning: Increased Co content reduces the NiO band gap and introduces transition-metal d–d channels and charge-transfer states, which increases interband transition density and can enhance nonlinear absorption (e.g., two-photon absorption) and refraction (Kerr-like) contributions. Structural co-segregation (e.g., Co3O4 formation upon annealing) further modifies density of states and defect-related transitions that control χ(3) magnitude and spectral position <cite id="0c0c876a-1">The optical energy gap of NiO thin films decreased as cobalt content increased</cite><cite id="0c0c876a-4">Upon annealing, mixed Co/Ni oxide separates into NiO and Co3O4 with distinct bandgaps</cite>.
- Carrier- and defect-mediated effects: Doping-induced changes in carrier concentration (via Burstein–Moss effect) and defect density alter linear and nonlinear optical properties. In Co-doped oxides, reduced Eg with doping can increase free-carrier concentration in the conduction band, modifying refraction via thermo-optic and plasma frequency mechanisms and changing absorption thresholds; morphology/grain size reductions also influence scattering and the effective nonlinear path length <cite id="8857b702-0">Doping with Co results in variations in the optical energy band gap; according to the Burstein–Moss effect, the Eg value increases with the strength of carrier concentration in the conduction band; Co doping in ZnO thin films has been restricted to low concentrations; under CW illumination, self-focusing/self-defocusing are associated with thermo-optic nonlinearities; we attempted to dope Co and study NLO properties using Z-scan</cite><cite id="0c0c876a-0">NiO film with 1% Zn doping exhibits a higher χ(3) value… attributed to increased nonlinear absorption and refractive index, possibly induced by electronic processes and local heating; higher surface roughness scatters light and decreases NLO response; crystallite size and defect states contribute</cite>.
- Concentration “sweet spots”: In closely related NiO:Zn systems, a modest dopant concentration (~1 at.%) maximizes χ(3) while higher roughness or carrier-screening effects can suppress gains; the synergy between defect states, crystallite size, and surface morphology explains concentration dependence and suggests similar trade-offs for Co-doped NiO <cite id="0c0c876a-0">NiO film with 1% Zn doping exhibits a higher χ(3) value; increased nonlinear susceptibility may result from greater presence of nickel and oxygen defect states; crystallite size and reduced surface roughness enhance response</cite>.

4) Expected evolution of χ(3), n2, and absorption with Co content in Ni/NiO hosts
- Low Co content: Expect increased band gap narrowing and defect-state density in NiO, boosting nonlinear absorption and refraction components. Z-scan should show self-defocusing (negative n2) with measurable χ(3) and possible saturable absorption onset, analogous to NiO:Cu/Cr/Fe where lensing persists and SA/DSA features appear with dopant identity and concentration <cite id="0c0c876a-1">The optical energy gap of NiO thin films decreased as cobalt content increased</cite><cite id="0a837950-2">Z-scan curves illustrate saturable absorption with valleys at z = 0; reverse saturable absorption is corroborated depending on dopant</cite>.
- Intermediate Co content: As Co increases (toward equimolar ratios in Co/Ni oxide), phase separation into NiO and Co3O4 and continued grain-size reduction can sustain or slightly diminish χ(3) due to parallel pathways and possible carrier screening. Z-scan metrics (n2, β) and χ(3) magnitudes typically peak at optimal composition, then decline as excessive doping induces disorder or percolation of conducting pathways; optical limiting and pulse-limiting behavior are often observed under pulsed excitation due to dynamic nonlinear absorption <cite id="0a837950-4">NiO and doped variants are promising candidates for optical limiting applications to protect sensitive devices from harmful laser exposure</cite><cite id="0c0c876a-4">Annealed films separate into NiO and Co3O4 with distinct bandgaps, reflecting composition-driven electronic structure changes</cite>.
- High Co content: Further Co addition can increase free-carrier concentration (reducing Eg) and introduce magnetic-dipolar or defect-related losses; morphology degradation (smaller grains, rougher surfaces) and defect-assisted trap states may dominate, reducing n2 magnitude and shifting absorption onsets. In Co/Ni oxide, the emergence of Co3O4 phase (with different spinel band structure) often correlates with changes in optical limiting and spectral selectivity relative to pure NiO <cite id="8857b702-0">Under CW illumination, self-focusing and self-defocusing are associated with thermo-optic nonlinearities; the Burstein–Moss effect ties increased carrier concentration to Eg changes</cite><cite id="0c0c876a-4">Phase separation into cubic NiO and cubic Co3O4 upon annealing</cite>.

5) Device implications and application windows
- Optical limiting and protection: Doped NiO systems exhibit optical power limiting and can act as effective limiters under pulsed excitation; Co-doping is expected to widen the spectral window and adjust threshold power by tuning absorption saturation dynamics, as demonstrated in transition-metal doped NiO systems (Cu, Cr, Fe) with quantified n2 and χ(3) enhancing limiters’ robustness <cite id="0a837950-4">Pulsed excitation… these samples acted as effective optical limiters; NiO and its doped variants are promising candidates for optical limiting applications</cite>.
- Saturable reflectors/absorbers: Z-scan reveals both saturable absorption (valley at z = 0) and reverse saturable absorption depending on dopant and concentration, indicating potential for ultrafast saturable absorbers when the imaginary part of χ(3) dominates; Co-doped systems can be engineered to favor SA or RSA by controlling Co content, crystallite size, and defect passivation <cite id="0a837950-2">Z-scan curves illustrate saturable absorption behavior with a distinct valley at z = 0; reverse saturable absorption is corroborated by valleys in corresponding doped samples</cite>.
- Band-engineered photonic materials: By tracking band gap versus Co content and phase evolution (ellipsometry and XRD), one can design composition windows where χ(3) magnitude peaks with minimal loss; mixed Co/Ni oxide films show how composition maps to phase-separated NiO/Co3O4, guiding annealing/doping strategies for targeted NLO performance <cite id="0c0c876a-4">Deposited and annealed Co/Ni oxide films characterized by XRD/ellipsometry; phase separation into NiO and Co3O4 with bandgap determination</cite>.

6) Practical guidance for studying Co-doped Ni (or NiO) at different concentrations
- Start with dilute Co (≤1–5 at.%) in NiO nanoparticles/films to emulate successful Zn-doping paradigms where ~1% maximized χ(3), then stepwise increase to 10–20 at.% to probe band-gap narrowing and phase evolution. Use XRD/Raman/ellipsometry to verify structure and Eg; correlate with Z-scan at 532/800/1064 nm for n2, β, and χ(3) sign/magnitude <cite id="0c0c876a-0">NiO film with 1% Zn doping exhibits a higher χ(3) value; defect states, crystallite size, and roughness influence response</cite><cite id="0c0c876a-4">Different Co/Ni compositions yield distinct phases and bandgaps post-annealing</cite>.
- Control synthesis variables (precursor stoichiometry, annealing temperature/time) to minimize morphology degradation with doping; surface passivation and crystallite size management can prevent scattering losses that suppress χ(3) at higher dopant levels <cite id="0c0c876a-0">Reduced surface roughness increases nonlinear response; crystallite size and defect states contribute to χ(3)</cite>.
- Expect self-defocusing (negative n2) from thermal and electronic contributions in NiO-like hosts; look for SA/DSA features and power-dependent transmittance modulation. Quantify χ(3) via Z-scan fits and track how n2 and β evolve with Co content; compare to undoped NiO to isolate Co-specific effects <cite id="0a837950-4">Negative n2 and self-defocusing behavior in NiO NPs with quantifiable transmittance modulation</cite><cite id="0a837950-2">Z-scan-derived χ(3) and identification of SA/DSA features in doped NiO</cite>.
- Consider pulsed characterization to expose dynamic effects (two-photon absorption, thermal effects) that drive optical limiting and saturable reflectivity; Co-doped systems with narrower Eg and higher defect densities often show strong pulsed-laser limiting at moderate peak intensities <cite id="0a837950-4">In pulsed excitation, these samples acted as effective optical limiters</cite>.

7) Limitations and open questions
- Direct, comprehensive Co-in-Ni concentration series with full χ(3)(ω) mapping is less documented than analogous Cu/Cr/Fe doping in NiO; however, mechanistic parallels (band gap reduction, defect-state creation, morphology change) and Co/Ni oxide phase diagrams support extrapolation. Future work should report Co content-dependent Z-scan across multiple wavelengths to resolve sign changes (self-focusing to self-defocusing), threshold powers for SA/TPA, and spectral selectivity as Co fraction varies <cite id="0c0c876a-1">Cobalt-doping reduces Eg and alters lattice/grain size in NiO-like systems</cite><cite id="0c0c876a-4">Co/Ni oxide composition evolves into NiO + Co3O4 with annealing, altering optical constants</cite>.
- Interplay between crystallite size and surface scattering can mask intrinsic NLO trends; isolating composition effects from morphology requires matched-anneal protocols and in-situ/operando optical characterization during dopant ramping <cite id="0c0c876a-0">Crystallite size and reduced surface roughness significantly affect measured nonlinear response</cite>.

In summary, cobalt-doping of nickel-based hosts (especially NiO and Co/Ni oxide films) measurably enhances third-order NLO properties up to an optimal Co content, with mechanisms rooted in band-structure modification, defect-state creation, and morphology control; Z-scan provides quantitative access to n2, absorption coefficients, and χ(3), while optical limiting and saturable absorption behaviors open application pathways in protection and ultrafast photonics. The most robust performance typically occurs at low-to-modest Co fractions with careful control of crystallite size and phase purity, as supported by analogous studies in doped NiO and Co/Ni oxide systems <cite id="0c0c876a-0">NiO film with 1% Zn doping exhibits a higher χ(3) value, with defect states, crystallite size, and roughness playing key roles</cite><cite id="0c0c876a-1">Cobalt-doping decreases Eg and grain size in NiO-like matrices, consistent with enhanced NLO tunability</cite><cite id="0c0c876a-4">Co/Ni oxide films evolve into NiO and Co3O4 with annealing, enabling band-gap-tuned NLO behavior</cite><cite id="0a837950-2">Z-scan reveals SA/DSA and allows quantitative extraction of n2 and χ(3) in doped NiO</cite><cite id="0a837950-4">NiO and doped variants demonstrate effective optical limiting under pulsed excitation</cite>.

Title: Investigation of Nonlinear Optical Properties of NiO Nanoparticles using the Z-Scan Technique
Snippet: Because of their enormous optical nonlinearity and short reaction time, the study of the nonlinear optical characteristics of semiconductor NPs has received significant interest [10]. The NPs exhibit electrical, optical, and magnetic characteristics that are distinct from those of their bulk counterparts, making them more desirable [11]. Nonlinear optical properties for several nanomaterials, including TiO2 NPs [12], ZnO NPs [13], Fe3O4 NPs [14], and MgO NPs [15], have been studied. NiO, a semiconductor with a significant band gap (around 4.0 eV), has been considered an attractive material for many technological applications [16]. It has been used as a transparent conducting material of the p-type in spin-valve devices [17] and electrochromic devices [18], as well as in photocatalysis, batteries, and chemical sensing [19]. Observed nonlinear optical effects include the electro-optical Kerr effect, the electro-optical Pokel effect, the Third Harmonic Generation (THG), the Second Harmonic Generation (SHG), self-focusing, nonlinear absorption, Two-Photon Absorption (TPA), Saturable Absorption (SA), and Reverse Saturable Absorption (RSA) [20]. There are several methods for measuring the nonlinear optical characteristics of materials, such as two-photon-induced fluorescence, self-phase modulation, four-wave mixing, pump-probe, and Z-scan methods [21]. The Z-scan technique, introduced by Sheik-Bahae et al. for the first time [22], is undoubtedly the most common, highly accurate method for characterizing the third-order nonlinear optical characteristics of samples. It is a reasonably straightforward method for determining both nonlinear refractive index and nonlinear absorption coefficient since it is based on a single measurement of beam distortion. The Z-scan consists of two parts: closed aperture and open aperture. Closed-aperture Z-scan measures the sign and magnitude of the materials' nonlinear refractive index. While the open aperture Z-scan measures the nonlinear absorption coefficient [23]. 

There are several reports on nanomaterials' nonlinear optical characteristics.

Title: Study on The Third-Order NLO Properties of Trace Metal Ions in Nitric Acid Solution by Closed-Aperture Z-scan Technique
Snippet: Introduction The need for novel material with relatively high nonlinear optical (NLO) behaviour has caused increasing interest in the field of photonics due to its potential in applications in diverse areas such as optical data storage [1], telecommunications [2], and information processing [3]. Title: Synthesis of Au, Ag, Curcumin Au/Ag, and Au-Ag Nanoparticles and Their Nonlinear Refractive Index Properties
Snippet: Metallic nanoparticles have attracted a huge interest because their physical and chemical properties are different from those of their bulks [1]. As a result they are ideal candidates for many applications, including electronics and optoelectronic devices, and in medical applications such as diagnosis, drug delivery, and therapy. Metallic nanoparticles form district energy levels, which are shown in the linear absorption spectra by a broad band absorption. This manifests as surface plasmon resonance, which does not exist in the case of bulk materials. Nanoparticles have a large number of conduction electrons. There are more atoms at the surface of the nanoparticles than the number of atoms inside, and thus this property gives rise to interesting properties due to the interaction between nanoparticles and surrounding media. The strong interaction of nanoparticles with light waves takes place because the conduction electrons on the metal surface undergo a combined oscillation when excited by light at specific wavelengths. The collective oscillation of excited electrons in the conduction band also known as surface plasmon resonance (SPR) and the surface area to volume ratio leads to a strong interaction with the incoming electromagnetic wave to enhance the local field, thus boosting the nonlinear optical properties of these materials. The optical properties of nanoparticles are strongly dependent on the particle size and shape and dielectric properties of the matrix. These properties have a vital role in developing optical devices and in the biomedical field. It has been suggested that, in the vicinity of the SPR absorption region, the nanoparticles exhibit a large value of optical nonlinearities. Different techniques have been used to investigate the optical nonlinearities such as four-wave mixing [2], nonlinear interferometry [3], and z-scan [4,5]. Z-scan is the most popular technique due to its simplicity and it allows the determination of the sign and the magnitude of nonlinear optical properties, such as nonlinear refractive index and nonlinear absorption in a single scan. Many reports have described the nonlinear properties and behavior demonstrated by nanoparticles and their dependence on sizes, shapes, and surrounding medium [6][7][8][9].

Title: Nonlinear Coefficient Determination of Au/Pd Bimetallic Nanoparticles Using Z-Scan
Snippet: In this paper we present the nonlinear optical characterization of Au/Pd nanoparticles in order to obtain the nonlinear refractive indices using the Z-scan technique. The experiments were performed using a 514 nm laser beam Ar+, with 14 Hz of modulation frequency, as excitation source. By using a lens the excitation beam was focused to a small spot and the sample was moved across the focal region along the z-axis by a motorized translation stage. Seven samples with different concentration ratio of Au/Pd nanoparticles were prepared by simultaneous reduction of gold and palladium ions in presence of poly (N-vinyl-2-pirrolidone) (PVP) using ethanol as a reducing agent. In this work, we report the application of the Z-scan technique, to generate optical transmission of laser light as a function of the z position for solutions containing bimetallic nanoparticles of Au (core)/Pd (shell) with average sizes ranging from 3 to 5 nm. The magnitude of the obtained nonlinear refractive index was in the order of 10?8 cm2/W. Our results show that the nonlinear refractive index has a nonlinear behavior when the (Au/Pd) ratio was increased.

documents.title: Study on The Third-Order NLO Properties of Trace Metal Ions in Nitric Acid Solution by Closed-Aperture Z-scan Technique
documents.snippet:
Introduction The need for novel material with relatively high nonlinear optical (NLO) behaviour has caused increasing interest in the field of photonics due to its potential in applications in diverse areas such as optical data storage [1], telecommunications [2], and information processing [3]. Many materials including organic and inorganic types have been studied for its third-order NLO susceptibility, due to the high demand from industrial sectors [4]. To date, various nonlinear properties and behaviour exhibited by metal nanoparticles (NPs) have been reported. Metal nanoparticles with relatively high third order nonlinearity have been extensively investigated, for instance gold [5,6] and silver [7,8]. On top of that, many researches related to heavy metals such as, calcium-halide [9], metal-organic e.g. dibromo(4-hydroxy-L-proline)cadmium (II) [10], Ni(II) [11] and metal Nitride e.g. TiN [12] were studied towards NLO response. In this study, five different metal ions of Pb Zn, Al, Cd and Hg in nitric acid solution were selected to its study its third order NLO response. 

A single beam Z-scan technique based on diode pump solid state laser with excitation wavelength of 532nm were utilized for nonlinear characterization due to its ability to determine the nonlinearity of different heavy metal samples in the form of liquid solution. Another reason Z-scan technique is preferable in this research over other nonlinear setups is that the general conditions that are easily fulfilled, data analysis is quick and simple, making it a good method for screening on both NLO responses from absorption and refraction in solids and liquids [13,14]. On top of that, this technique also able to provide values of third-order nonlinear susceptibility߯ (3) , simultaneously along with its magnitude and sign. In this research, we report the value of nonlinear refractive index, and real part of third-order nonlinear susceptibility, ߯ (3) of five different heavy metals samples.

documents.title: Synthesis of Au, Ag, Curcumin Au/Ag, and Au-Ag Nanoparticles and Their Nonlinear Refractive Index Properties
documents.snippet: Metallic nanoparticles have attracted a huge interest because their physical and chemical properties are different from those of their bulks [1]. As a result they are ideal candidates for many applications, including electronics and optoelectronic devices, and in medical applications such as diagnosis, drug delivery, and therapy. Metallic nanoparticles form district energy levels, which are shown in the linear absorption spectra by a broad band absorption. This manifests as surface plasmon resonance, which does not exist in the case of bulk materials. Nanoparticles have a large number of conduction electrons. There are more atoms at the surface of the nanoparticles than the number of atoms inside, and thus this property gives rise to interesting properties due to the interaction between nanoparticles and surrounding media. The strong interaction of nanoparticles with light waves takes place because the conduction electrons on the metal surface undergo a combined oscillation when excited by light at specific wavelengths. The collective oscillation of excited electrons in the conduction band also known as surface plasmon resonance (SPR) and the surface area to volume ratio leads to a strong interaction with the incoming electromagnetic wave to enhance the local field, thus boosting the nonlinear optical properties of these materials. The optical properties of nanoparticles are strongly dependent on the particle size and shape and dielectric properties of the matrix. These properties have a vital role in developing optical devices and in the biomedical field. It has been suggested that, in the vicinity of the SPR absorption region, the nanoparticles exhibit a large value of optical nonlinearities. Different techniques have been used to investigate the optical nonlinearities such as four-wave mixing [2], nonlinear interferometry [3], and z-scan [4,5]. Z-scan is the most popular technique due to its simplicity and it allows the determination of the sign and the magnitude of nonlinear optical properties, such as nonlinear refractive index and nonlinear absorption in a single scan. Many reports have described the nonlinear properties and behavior demonstrated by nanoparticles and their dependence on sizes, shapes, and surrounding medium [6][7][8][9].

documents.title: Nonlinear Coefficient Determination of Au/Pd Bimetallic Nanoparticles Using Z-Scan
documents.snippet: In this paper we present the nonlinear optical characterization of Au/Pd nanoparticles in order to obtain the nonlinear refractive indices using the Z-scan technique. The experiments were performed using a 514 nm laser beam Ar+, with 14 Hz of modulation frequency, as excitation source. By using a lens the excitation beam was focused to a small spot and the sample was moved across the focal region along the z-axis by a motorized translation stage. Seven samples with different concentration ratio of Au/Pd nanoparticles were prepared by simultaneous reduction of gold and palladium ions in presence of poly (N-vinyl-2-pirrolidone) (PVP) using ethanol as a reducing agent. In this work, we report the application of the Z-scan technique, to generate optical transmission of laser light as a function of the z position for solutions containing bimetallic nanoparticles of Au (core)/Pd (shell) with average sizes ranging from 3 to 5 nm. The magnitude of the obtained nonlinear refractive index was in the order of 10?8 cm2/W. Our results show that the nonlinear refractive index has a nonlinear behavior when the (Au/Pd) ratio was increased.
